chapters.title: Steady Heat Conduction
chapters.desc: Thermal resistance networks for walls, pipes and spheres; contact resistance; critical insulation radius; fins; shape factors.

cards.h: Steady conduction in a plane wall
cards.t: When the two faces of a wall stay at fixed temperatures and nothing changes with time, the heat rate is the same at every plane inside the wall. With constant \(k\) and no generation, the temperature drops linearly through the thickness.

Writing the wall result as temperature difference over resistance gives an analogy with Ohm’s law: \(\Delta T\) plays the role of voltage, \(\dot Q\) of current. A thicker wall or a poorer conductor means a larger resistance.

Convection from a surface can also be written as a resistance. Radiation is handled the same way with a radiation heat transfer coefficient \(h_\text{rad}\); when both act in parallel on the same surface they can be merged into a combined coefficient.

Heat flowing from a fluid, through a wall, into another fluid passes through resistances in series, so they add. The temperature drop across any layer equals the heat rate times that layer’s resistance. The overall coefficient \(U\) packs the whole network into one number.

For walls made of several layers, each layer adds its own \(L/kA\) term in series. Once \(\dot Q\) is known, the temperature at any interface follows by stepping through the network one resistance at a time.

Real surfaces are rough, so two solids pressed together touch only at peaks; the gaps hold air or another fluid. This adds an extra temperature drop at the interface, described by a thermal contact conductance \(h_c\). It can be reduced by higher pressure, smoother surfaces or a thermal grease.

Layers that sit side by side (each spanning the full thickness) carry heat in parallel: their conductances add, like parallel electrical resistors. Combined series–parallel networks are built from these two rules, assuming heat flow stays approximately one-dimensional.

In a pipe wall or a spherical shell the area changes with radius, but in steady operation the heat rate through every layer is the same. The resistance depends on the ratio or difference of the radii.
cards.eq: R_\text{cyl} = \frac{\ln(r_2/r_1)}{2\pi Lk},\qquad R_\text{sph} = \frac{r_2 - r_1}{4\pi r_1 r_2 k}

cards.t: An insulated pipe is a chain: inner convection, pipe wall, insulation, outer convection. Add the resistances in series. In a typical steam pipe the metal wall’s resistance is tiny and the insulation dominates.
cards.ex: Textbook Example 3–8 pattern: \(R_\text{total} = R_\text{conv,1} + R_\text{pipe} + R_\text{ins} + R_\text{conv,2}\), then \(\dot Q = (T_{\infty1}-T_{\infty2})/R_\text{total}\).

cards.t: Insulating a small pipe or wire increases conduction resistance but also enlarges the outer surface, which lowers convection resistance. Below a critical outer radius, adding insulation actually increases heat loss; the loss peaks at the critical radius.

Fins add surface area to increase convection. A steady energy balance on a thin slice of a fin with constant cross-section gives a second-order equation for the excess temperature \(\theta = T - T_\infty\).

Two tip conditions give simple closed forms. In a very long fin the tip reaches the fluid temperature. If the tip loses negligible heat, it is treated as insulated, and the result picks up a \(\tanh mL\) factor.
cards.eq: \dot Q_\text{long} = \sqrt{hpkA_c}\,(T_b - T_\infty),\qquad \dot Q_\text{adiabatic tip} = \sqrt{hpkA_c}\,(T_b - T_\infty)\tanh mL

cards.t: Convection from the fin tip can be included by using the adiabatic-tip formula with a slightly longer fin. For a rectangular fin of thickness \(t\), \(L_c = L + t/2\); for a pin fin of diameter \(D\), \(L_c = L + D/4\).

Fin efficiency compares the actual heat rate with the ideal one if the whole fin were at the base temperature. It drops as \(mL\) grows, because the far end of a long fin is close to the fluid temperature.

Effectiveness compares heat transfer with the fin to heat transfer from the same base area without it. Fins pay off most with high \(k\), thin cross-sections (large \(p/A_c\)) and low \(h\), which is why they are used on the gas side of heat exchangers.
Many two- and three-dimensional steady problems (buried pipes, pipes in walls, cubes) have been solved once and tabulated as a conduction shape factor \(S\), which depends only on geometry.

quiz.q: Two layers of a wall are in series. Their thermal resistances…
quiz.why: In series the same heat rate passes through each layer, so the temperature drops and therefore the resistances add (Eq. 3–16).

quiz.q: Which change lowers the thermal resistance L/(kA) of a plane wall?
quiz.why: Resistance falls as area or conductivity rise; the temperature difference does not appear in R (Eq. 3–5).

quiz.q: For a cylindrical layer, the conduction resistance is…
quiz.why: Eq. 3–39. The spherical-shell form is Eq. 3–41.

quiz.q: Adding insulation to a thin wire whose outer radius is below k/h will…
options: increase heat loss until the critical radius
make the wire hotter only at night
quiz.why: Below the critical radius (Eq. 3–50) the larger convecting surface outweighs the added conduction resistance.

quiz.q: Fin efficiency for an adiabatic-tip fin is…
quiz.why: Eq. 3–77; it tends to 1 as mL → 0 and falls as the fin gets longer.

chapters.title: Transient Heat Conduction
chapters.desc: Lumped systems and the Biot number; one-term solutions for walls, cylinders and spheres; semi-infinite solids; product solutions.

cards.t: If a body’s interior stays nearly uniform in temperature while it heats or cools, its temperature depends on time only. An energy balance equating convection at the surface to the change in stored energy gives an exponential approach to the fluid temperature.

cards.h: Biot number and the lumped criterion
cards.t: The Biot number compares conduction resistance inside the body with convection resistance at its surface, using the characteristic length \(L_c = V/A_s\). Lumped analysis is accepted when Bi is no more than about 0.1.

cards.h: Heat transferred in a lumped body
cards.t: Once \(T(t)\) is known, the instantaneous rate follows from Newton’s law of cooling, and the total energy exchanged is the change in stored energy. The maximum possible occurs when the body reaches the fluid temperature.
cards.eq: \dot Q(t) = hA_s[T(t)-T_\infty],\quad Q = mc_p[T(t)-T_i],\quad Q_\text{max} = mc_p(T_\infty - T_i)

cards.t: When Bi is large, the inside lags the surface and temperature depends on both position and time. Large plane walls, long cylinders and spheres are treated as one-dimensional problems with convection at the surface.

Writing the problem in dimensionless form collapses many parameters into three: position \(X = x/L\), the Biot number and the Fourier number (dimensionless time). Here the Biot number uses the half-thickness \(L\) or radius \(r_o\), not \(V/A_s\).
The exact series solutions converge quickly. For \(\tau > 0.2\), keeping only the first term gives errors under about 2 percent. Constants \(\lambda_1\) and \(A_1\) depend on Bi and are tabulated.
The most heat a body can exchange is its full change in stored energy. The fraction transferred by time \(t\) follows from the centre temperature with geometry-specific expressions.

A body that extends far enough that its far side never feels a surface change, such as the ground under a road or a thick block heated briefly, is semi-infinite. One similarity variable combines position and time.
If the surface is suddenly raised to \(T_s\), the temperature inside follows the complementary error function, and the surface heat flux falls off as \(1/\sqrt t\).

When two large bodies at different temperatures touch, the interface instantly reaches a fixed temperature, weighted by each body’s \(\sqrt{k\rho c_p}\). That is why metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature.

Short cylinders, rectangular bars and similar shapes can be handled by multiplying one-dimensional solutions: the dimensionless temperature of the 2-D or 3-D body is the product of those of the intersecting plane walls, cylinders or semi-infinite solids.

quiz.q: Lumped system analysis is acceptable when…
quiz.why: With Bi ≤ 0.1 the interior temperature stays nearly uniform (Sec. 4–1, Eq. 4–9).

quiz.q: The characteristic length used in lumped analysis is…
quiz.why: Lc = V/As for lumped analysis; the exact 1-D solutions instead use L or r_o (Sec. 4–2).

quiz.q: A larger b = hA_s/(ρVc_p) means the body…
quiz.why: Temperature approaches T∞ as e^(−bt), so a larger b means a faster response (Eqs. 4–4, 4–5).

quiz.q: The one-term approximation is accurate (error under about 2%) when…
quiz.why: The higher series terms die out quickly; for τ > 0.2 the first term suffices (Sec. 4–2).

quiz.q: Metal feels colder than wood at the same temperature mainly because metal has a larger…
quiz.why: The contact temperature is weighted by √(kρc_p) (Eq. 4–49), so the metal pulls the interface toward its own temperature.

chapters.title: Numerical Methods in Heat Conduction
chapters.desc: Finite differences for steady 1-D and 2-D conduction, boundary nodes, explicit and implicit transient methods and their stability.

cards.t: Analytical solutions need simple geometry, constant properties and simple boundary conditions. Numerical methods relax these limits, allow more realistic models and are flexible enough to explore design changes. Their results still need judgment: a solver cannot replace understanding.
A derivative is replaced by a difference over a small step \(\Delta x\). Dropping the higher terms of the Taylor series gives the error of the approximation, which shrinks as the step gets smaller.

The medium is divided into nodes a distance \(\Delta x\) apart. An energy balance on the volume around each interior node, or the difference form of the second derivative, gives one algebraic equation per node.

A boundary node owns only half a volume element. Its equation comes from an energy balance that includes whatever crosses the surface: a specified flux, convection, radiation, or nothing for an insulated surface.
cards.eq: hA(T_\infty - T_0) + kA\,\frac{T_1 - T_0}{\Delta x} + \dot e_0\,\frac{A\Delta x}{2} = 0

cards.t: An insulated boundary or a symmetry line behaves like a mirror: imagine the node on the other side with the same temperature as its reflection. The boundary node can then be treated as an interior node.

On a square mesh (\(\Delta x = \Delta y = l\)), an interior node’s temperature satisfies a simple balance with its four neighbours. Without heat generation, each node is the average of its neighbours.
Curved or slanted boundaries can be approximated by a fine staircase of rectangular cells, or treated with energy balances on the actual partial volume elements next to the boundary.

Transient problems are marched forward in time steps \(\Delta t\). The explicit method evaluates the heat flows at the known time step \(i\), so each new temperature comes directly. The implicit method uses the new step \(i+1\), so the equations must be solved together.

The dimensionless mesh Fourier number links the time step to the space step. In 1-D with the explicit method, each interior node’s new temperature is a weighted mix of its old value and its neighbours.
cards.eq: \tau = \frac{\alpha\,\Delta t}{\Delta x^2},\qquad T_m^{i+1} = \tau(T_{m-1}^i + T_{m+1}^i) + (1-2\tau)T_m^i + \tau\,\frac{\dot e_m^i\,\Delta x^2}{k}

cards.t: The explicit method can oscillate and blow up if the time step is too large. The coefficient of \(T_m^i\) must not be negative, which limits \(\tau\): \(\tau \le 1/2\) for 1-D interior nodes and \(\tau \le 1/4\) in 2-D. The implicit method is unconditionally stable.

Results carry discretization error (from replacing derivatives by differences) and round-off error (from finite digits). Smaller steps cut discretization error but add more arithmetic and more round-off; refine until results stop changing meaningfully.

quiz.q: The finite difference form of d²T/dx² at node m is…
quiz.why: Eq. 5–9: the difference of two first-derivative differences, divided by Δx.

quiz.q: With no heat generation, a 2-D interior node on a square mesh has a temperature equal to…
options: the average of its four neighbours
quiz.why: From Eq. 5–35 with ė = 0: 4T_node equals the sum of the four neighbours.

quiz.q: For 1-D interior nodes, the explicit method is stable when…
quiz.why: The coefficient 1 − 2τ of T_m^i must not be negative (Eq. 5–52).

quiz.q: An insulated boundary node can be treated as an interior node by…
quiz.why: Reflect the neighbouring node across the insulated boundary (Sec. 5–3).
